Akhil I. went looking for a company to fund and ended up running the missing one. Watchtower Labs grew out of a military planning problem that followed an investor back to his own side of the table.

Upstarts Media reports that Iyer and Shield Capital founder Raj S. heard the need from Admiral Samuel Paparo: better logistics planning. When their search for an investment came up short, they built a company. That is a fairly demanding way to answer a customer request.

Watchtower emerged from stealth on October 21 with $35M in Seed financing, co-led by Shield Capital and Conviction, with Founders Fund and IQT participating. Shield incubated the business. Iyer, a former Marine special operations officer and Shield investor, became co-founder and CEO.

Alongside Iyer are co-founder and CTO Suren Aghajanyan and co-founder and Head of Engineering John Morman, both former Microsoft engineering leaders. Their task starts with the arithmetic behind a military operation: fuel, transport, spare parts, munitions, routes and time.

A commander can have several plausible courses of action and resources for only some of them. Then a delivery slips or a route changes, and the staff has to work through the consequences again. The useful answer includes the assumptions that made a recommendation possible.

Watchtower combines AI, simulation and optimization to help planners explore those choices. Conviction describes language models interpreting the request while deterministic engines perform the calculations. Watchtower says its system exposes the constraints and tradeoffs behind options, with people retaining decision authority. That division of labor matters to the buyer: an officer needs to challenge a plan's fuel or transport assumptions without having to reverse-engineer a fluent paragraph from an AI assistant.

There is already a government procurement path underneath the launch. The Defense Innovation Unit confirms Watchtower received a January 2026 prototype contract through its Joint Sustainment Decision Tool program. The program also includes other suppliers, giving military buyers alternatives as the tools develop.

The financing will support hiring, more applications, testing and deployment. As Watchtower reaches into broader operational planning, its engineers will keep meeting the officer whose recommendation depends on the next resupply arriving. Every new application adds another set of assumptions that person needs to see.

An AI interviewer inside a payroll suite will be convenient, and convenience is how nobody ends up reading the scoring logic.

Dayforce announced it has signed an agreement to acquire Ribbon, a Toronto company that runs AI screening interviews. Dayforce says Ribbon is proven at scale, with hundreds of customers and over one million completed interviews. Terms weren't disclosed. Those are real numbers to have built, and credit to Ribbon for getting there.

I build a competing product at Ployo (ployo.ai), 30,000+ AI interviews so far, so weigh this accordingly. My read, and I could be wrong: interviewing is about to move from a tool somebody chose on purpose to a checkbox inside the system a company already pays for.

That's great for procurement. One contract, one login, one data trail.

It's harder on the question I'd want a TA lead asking in every demo. When a candidate gets a low score, can a recruiter read why in plain words, and overrule it without raising a ticket? A feature bundled into a suite tends to get judged on whether it switches on, not on whether anyone can inspect it.

Whoever owns the rubric owns the hire. Make sure that's still you.

😄 Friday Humour: The Mysterious Architecture of Modern Hiring!
When ATS Says YES, Recruiter Says YES, but Hiring Manager Says… MAYBE! 😂
A hypothetical story from the world of technology recruitment!
Phase 1: The Perfect Match ❤️
🤖 ATS: Resume shortlisted! 95% skills match!
📞 Talent Hunter (TH): "Your profile looks fantastic! Exactly what we're looking for in an Enterprise Architect."
👨‍💻 Candidate: "Wonderful! This aligns perfectly with my experience."
TH explains the cloud transformation, Enterprise Architecture strategy and AI initiatives.
A match made in the cloud! ☁️
Phase 2: The Great Interrogation 🎙️
TH: "Tell me about yourself."
Candidate: "Sure! I have 20+ years of experience..."
🎙️ Recording started. AI transcription enabled.
Then come the classics:
✅ Recent projects and responsibilities?
✅ Cloud, Data and AI expertise?
✅ Work authorization?
✅ Salary expectations?
✅ Remote/hybrid preference?
✅ Availability?
TH: "Excellent! The Hiring Manager is looking for someone like you!"
Candidate: "Great! Looking forward to the technical round."
Phase 3: Distributed Silence Architecture 🤐
Week 1: No updates.
Week 2: Still no updates.
Candidate sends follow-up #1, #2, #3...
Apparently, recruitment entered serverless mode — no server, no response! 😂
Phase 4: The Plot Twist 🎬
Finally, an email arrives!
📩 TH: "The Hiring Manager was impressed with your experience. However, we've selected someone whose background is more closely aligned with the requirements."
Candidate: 🤔
"Interesting! Two weeks ago, my experience was exactly what you needed. Did the JD undergo a production deployment without change approval?"
Phase 5: Root Cause Analysis 🔍
As an Enterprise Architect, the candidate investigates:
1️⃣ Internal Candidate Pattern: Was someone already identified while external recruitment served as a compliance checkbox?
2️⃣ Dynamic Requirements Pattern: Did the JD change after screening? No version history! 😂
3️⃣ Recruiter–HM Integration Failure: Were TH and HM operating on different schemas? API contract mismatch!
4️⃣ Referral-Based Routing: Did external candidates follow the standard pipeline while someone else had a private endpoint? 🚀
Final Architecture Review 🏁
ATS: PASS ✅
Recruiter: PASS ✅
Experience: IMPRESSIVE ✅
Technical Interview: NOT REQUIRED ❌
Selection Criteria: CLASSIFIED 🔒
Root Cause: Unknown. Observability: Zero.
Jokes aside, selecting a better-qualified candidate is fair. But inconsistent expectations, vague feedback and prolonged silence raise questions about transparency.
Modern recruitment needs more than AI-powered ATS and transcription.
It needs accountability, consistent criteria and honest communication.
After all, what's the point of AI in recruitment if we still can't debug human decision-making? 😂
Happy Friday!

Infosys added 4,480 employees. But it still lowered its growth forecast.

That's an interesting combination.

On October 23, Infosys reported its Q2 FY27 results.

The company added 4,480 employees, bringing its total headcount to 332,542.

Its AI revenue grew 29% quarter-on-quarter.

And it reported $5.2 billion in large deal wins.

Yet Infosys lowered its full-year revenue growth guidance to 1–2%, down from its previous 1.5–3% range.

So what does this tell us?

A company can hire people, win large contracts, and grow its AI business while still facing uncertainty about its overall growth.

And that's something worth understanding if you're working in technology, marketing, consulting, or business.

A company's growth story is rarely as simple as one positive number.

For employees, hiring announcements are encouraging. But they don't automatically tell you which skills will be in demand, which teams will grow, or how the business will evolve.

For job seekers, a company's expansion doesn't guarantee that every role is equally valuable or that hiring will continue at the same pace.

For managers, winning new business is only part of the challenge. Delivering those projects profitably, developing talent, and managing changing client expectations matter too.

And for business leaders, the question is whether the company is building sustainable growth, not simply increasing headcount or announcing impressive deal numbers.

That's why I pay attention to the combination of hiring, revenue, deal wins, and guidance.

One number tells you what happened.

The combination helps you understand the business.

Before celebrating a company's growth, look at what is growing, what is slowing down, and what management expects next.

That's a much better way to understand where a business might be heading.

1. JIO PLATFORMS IPO DRAWS RECORD DEMAND

Jio Platforms' Rs 30,213-crore IPO closed with 22.19 times subscription, attracting bids worth over Rs 4.9 lakh crore excluding the anchor book. Strong institutional interest signals appetite for India's digital infrastructure story. But oversubscription is not a guarantee of post-listing gains: investors must assess valuation, cash generation and competitive risks.

2. RBI REITERATES LISTING RULE FOR UPPER-LAYER NBFCS

RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra said upper-layer NBFCs accessing public funds must list, renewing attention on Tata Sons. The issue goes beyond one conglomerate: regulators want transparency where complex group structures and leverage may create systemic risks. Governance and market disclosure remain central to financial stability.

3. INFOSYS CUTS FY27 REVENUE OUTLOOK

Infosys lowered its constant-currency revenue growth forecast to 1-2% from 1.5-3%, even as Q2 net profit rose 6.2% to Rs 7,828 crore. Soft US demand and AI-related pricing pressure are challenging traditional IT services. The key question is whether AI-led contracts can offset pressure on legacy revenues.

4. BOND YIELDS EXTEND HISTORIC LOSING STREAK

India's benchmark 10-year government bond yield reached 7.47% after ten consecutive weeks of increases, the longest such run in three decades. Higher crude prices and global yields are adding pressure. Rising sovereign borrowing costs can affect corporate financing, valuations and the government's interest burden.

5. INDIA'S FLASH PMI HITS FOUR-MONTH HIGH

The HSBC flash composite PMI rose to 56.7 in October from 55.9 in September, supported by new orders and stronger services activity. A reading above 50 indicates expansion. Yet manufacturing hiring slowed, suggesting that stronger output does not automatically translate into proportionate job creation.

6. JSW STEEL PROFIT JUMPS 225%

JSW Steel reported Q2 consolidated net profit of Rs 5,279 crore, up 225.3% year-on-year, alongside revenue growth of 20.7%. Better volumes, price recovery and cost management helped earnings. Planned capacity expansion could support future demand, but coal costs, debt and steel-price volatility remain material risks.

7. PLFS TO CAPTURE GIG AND UNPAID WORK

The government proposes revising the Periodic Labour Force Survey from January 2027 to better count platform workers and unpaid caregiving and household work. Better measurement can improve labour policy and reveal overlooked economic contributions, particularly by women. Survey design and consistent data collection will determine its value.

Day 7/30: Managing Renewal Risk in B2B SaaS 

How do you save a £42,000 account when the customer is questioning your product's value and considering a cheaper competitor?

 In today's Scenario,
 The company is PayPilot, a fintech SaaS platform, and the customer is Sterling & Co.

Sterling & Co has used PayPilot for nine months. Invoice automation is widely adopted, but payment reconciliation (matching payments to invoices) is still a problem. With 60 days to renewal, the Finance Director is questioning the value of the subscription, recurring support tickets are adding to the concern, and a cheaper competitor is on the table.

My starting point: the recurring reconciliation tickets. They are the most likely reason behind the value doubt.

Here's how I'd approach the 60 days:
i. Investigate before assuming (Days 1-10): Revisit the customer's original objectives, review the tickets for patterns, and find out whether the gap is a product issue, a setup issue, or a workflow issue.

ii. Measure value, not logins: Reconciliation time, staff hours saved, automation rate, and transactions needing manual correction, compared against the pre-PayPilot baseline.

iii. Understand each stakeholder: The Finance Director needs clarity on the operational problem. The CFO needs the financial return in numbers. I'd also confirm early who signs the renewal.

iv. Build the retention plan (Days 10-45): Name the root cause, assign owners across Support, Product, and Engineering, set dated fixes, and send the customer weekly progress updates.

v. Handle the competitor and the discount request: I'd ask what the competitor offers that PayPilot doesn't, and compare on outcomes and cost of switching, not price alone. If asked to cut the contract from £42,000 to £30,000, I'd explore the real concern and the options I'm authorised to offer, with Sales and Finance involved, and never promise a discount I can't approve.

vi. Go into renewal with evidence (Days 45-60): Share a short value summary: what improved, what's still open, and the plan ahead.

My key takeaway: Retention isn't about convincing every customer to renew at any cost. It's about understanding what is stopping them from getting value, fixing the right problems, and helping them make an informed decision. A renewal conversation is far stronger when it rests on evidence, not assumptions.

Should their skills go unused simply because they cannot find a full-time position immediately?

✅ Explore remote work wherever legally and operationally feasible, subject to applicable immigration, employment, tax, and work-authorisation requirements.

Companies get access to experienced talent for defined business needs. Professionals get an opportunity to contribute, sustain their careers, and demonstrate their value.

This is not a request for charity. It is a call for a win-win business arrangement.

American companies have benefited enormously from the contributions of skilled professionals from across the world, including H-1B workers.

Today, some of these professionals need an opportunity to work. Tomorrow, their experience could help your company solve a difficult problem, deliver a delayed project, or build something new.

If you cannot offer a permanent job today, could you offer a meaningful contract?

The junior job is not coming back onshore. That is the story running through this week's labor data, and almost nobody is saying it out loud.

The Fed's October Beige Book finally described what AI is doing to employment. Not layoffs. Firms in five of twelve districts are letting people leave without replacing them and quietly not opening requisitions. Headcount plans are being revised downward with no announcement attached. Providers waiting for a client notice will wait forever, because attrition never files one.

Ireland put a number on where that lands. Entry-level hiring in AI-exposed occupations fell 16.2% year on year, against 10.8% for those occupations overall. Junior roles are falling half again as fast as the jobs that contain them. Canada lost 68,000 jobs in September and 48,000 belonged to workers under 25 — roughly 70% of the losses on a cohort that is about 13% of the workforce. Participation hit its lowest non-pandemic level since 1997, which means some of them stopped looking.

Meanwhile, 86% of the top 100 U.S. accounting firms now employ offshore staff. Up from 83% a year ago. Offshore workers average 8.2% of total headcount. And all 25 of the largest firms plan to increase their use.

That last figure is the one that matters. Unanimity means this stopped being a competitive choice and became a cost structure. A firm that does not offshore is now pricing against rivals who do.

Put the two halves together and the shape is clear: the junior work is not disappearing. It is relocating. The entry-level job that used to come with it is not being rebuilt onshore.

For Philippine BPO and staffing leaders, that reframes the opportunity. The demand is real and deepening. But it is shifting toward verified skills over credentials, and toward buyers who need certainty because their own planning horizon has shrunk. On the talent side, the ladder is being pulled up in Dublin and Toronto. It is being extended in Manila and Cebu — for those who can demonstrate capability before they are handed a seat.

The UK offers one flicker of contrast: permanent placements rose at their fastest pace in four years. But read the components. Salary growth is decelerating and candidate supply keeps climbing. That is a market clearing a backlog, not one competing for scarce people.

One more thing worth watching. Chile's Senate is weighing a bill that would ban subcontracting call center work performed outside the country — targeting the contract itself, not just disclosure obligations. Most offshoring restrictions regulate the buyer. That instrument is different, and it sets a precedent regardless of whether it passes.

The rungs are moving. The question is who is building the new ones.

→ Energy: +20.5%, tied with Banking for the steepest growth of any industry
→ AI/ML: +18.1%

Energy's growth is acquisition-led: 269 acquisitions and 175 new contracts.

AI still dominates volume, with 1,411 signals and 542 funding events (more than double any other industry's funding). 

But its pace is cooling.

Leadership is turning over in both. In the last 30 days: 43 CEO transitions in energy, 57 in AI/ML.

Why this matters for talent: every acquisition is an integration, and every new CEO brings a new plan. 

Both trigger restructuring, new hiring, and good people taking recruiter calls. These signals show up months before the job postings do.

AI and energy are now competing for the same short list of people. The companies that win won't be the ones posting fastest. 

They'll be the ones who mapped that talent 6–18 months ahead.

And an empty seat in a contested role costs far more than the salary: delayed projects, burned-out teams, and harder conversations with the board.
